english: Damn your eyes, damn your eyes.
danish_before_fix: Fanden tage dine øjne, fanden tage dine øjne.
danish_after_fix: Fanden tage jeres øjne, fanden tage jeres øjne.

english: “A disaster,” agreed Paul, leaping to his feet; and as they slid and scrambled down, he kept quoting the guidebook about “these islands being justly celebrated for their park-like prospects and the extent and variety of their marine curiosities.” But it wasn’t quite right, Andrew felt, picking his way down the cliff—all this shouting and damning your eyes, this slapping him on the back and calling him “old fellow” and the rest of it; it wasn’t quite right. That was the trouble with taking women on walks. On the beach they split up. Andrew went out onto the Pope’s Nose, took off his shoes, rolled his socks up inside them, and left that couple to look after themselves; Nancy waded out to rocks of her own and searched pools of her own and left that couple to look after themselves. Crouching low, she touched the smooth, rubbery sea anemones that clung like lumps of jelly to the side of the rock. Brooding, she made the pool into the sea, and the minnows into sharks and whales; she held her hand up against the sun and threw vast clouds over this tiny world, bringing darkness and desolation, like God himself, to millions of ignorant, innocent creatures; then all at once she pulled her hand away and let the sunlight pour down. Across the pale crisscrossed sand stalked some fantastic leviathan, high-stepping, fringed, gauntleted (she was still making the pool bigger), and slid into the vast cracks of the mountainside. And then, as her eyes slid imperceptibly up above the pool and came to rest on the wavering line where sea met sky, on the tree trunks that steamer smoke set wavering on the horizon, all that power sweeping savagely in and inevitably pulling back held her hypnotized. And the two sensations, of that hugeness and of this tininess (the pool had shrunk again), flowering inside it, made her feel tied hand and foot, unable to move, under the intensity of feelings that shrank her own body, her own life, and the lives of everyone in the world, forever, to nothing. So she brooded, crouched over the pool, listening to the waves.
danish_before_fix: »En katastrofe,« var Paul enig og sprang på benene; og mens de gled og kravlede ned, blev han ved med at citere rejsehåndbogen om »disse øer, der med rette er berømte for deres parklignende udsigter og de marine kuriositeters omfang og mangfoldighed.« Men det var ikke helt rigtigt, følte Andrew, mens han valgte sin vej ned ad klippen — alt det råberi og fanden-tage-dine-øjne, det med at klappe ham på ryggen og kalde ham »gamle dreng« og alt det der; det var ikke helt rigtigt. Det var problemet ved at tage kvinder med på vandretur. På stranden delte de sig. Andrew gik ud på Pavens Næse, tog sine sko af, rullede strømperne ind i dem og lod det par passe sig selv; Nancy vadede ud til sine egne sten og ledte i sine egne vandpytter og lod det par passe sig selv. Dybt nede på hug rørte hun ved de glatte, gummiagtige søanemoner, der klistrede som klumper af gelé fast til siden af klippen. Grublende gjorde hun vandpytten til havet og småfiskene til hajer og hvaler; hun løftede hånden op mod solen og kastede vældige skyer over denne bitte lille verden, så den fik mørke og ødelæggelse, som Gud selv, over millioner af uvidende, uskyldige skabninger; så trak hun pludselig hånden væk og lod sollyset strømme ned. Hen over den bleggule, krydsede sand listede et fantastisk havuhyre, højbenet, frynset, behandsket (hun var stadig i gang med at gøre vandpytten større), og gled ind i bjergsidens vældige sprækker. Og så, da hendes øjne umærkeligt gled op over vandpytten og faldt til ro på den svajende linje, hvor hav mødte himmel, på de træstammer, som dampskibsrøgen fik til at svaje ved horisonten, holdt al den magt, der fejede vildt ind og uafværgeligt trak sig tilbage, hende hypnotiseret. Og de to fornemmelser, af den vældighed og af denne ringhed (vandpytten var skrumpet ind igen), der blomstrede inde i hende, fik hende til at føle sig bundet på hænder og fødder, ude af stand til at røre sig, under intensiteten af følelser, der skrumpede hendes egen krop, hendes eget liv og alle verdens menneskers liv for evigt ind til intet. Så hun grublede, sammenkrøbet over vandpytten, og lyttede til bølgerne.

english: Well then, Nancy had gone with them, Mrs. Ramsay supposed. Putting down a brush, picking up a comb, and calling “Come in” at a tap on the door (Jasper and Rose came in), she wondered whether Nancy’s being with them made anything happening less likely or more likely. Less likely, somehow, Mrs. Ramsay felt—quite irrationally—though after all, disaster on such a scale wasn’t probable. They couldn’t all be drowned. And once again she felt herself alone, facing her old enemy, life.
danish_before_fix: Nå, Nancy var altså gået med dem, formodede fru Ramsay. Hun lagde en børste fra sig, tog en kam og råbte »Kom ind«, da det bankede på døren (Jasper og Rose kom ind), og spurgte sig selv, om det, at Nancy var med, gjorde det mindre eller mere sandsynligt, at der skete noget. Mindre sandsynligt, syntes fru Ramsay på en eller anden måde—ganske irrationelt—selv om en katastrofe i den størrelsesorden jo egentlig ikke var sandsynlig. De kunne ikke alle sammen drukne. Og endnu en gang følte hun sig alene, ansigt til ansigt med sin gamle fjende, livet.

english: And while Jasper took the message, she told Rose that, if she liked, she could pick out the jewels her mother would wear. With fifteen people sitting down to dinner, you can’t keep things waiting forever. Now she was starting to feel annoyed with them for being so late. It was thoughtless of them; and on top of her worry about them, it annoyed her that they should pick this very night to stay out late, when she particularly wanted the dinner to go well, since William Bankes had at last agreed to eat with them; and they were having Mildred’s masterpiece—Bœuf en Daube, a French beef stew slow-cooked in wine. Everything depended on dishes going to the table at the exact moment they were ready. The beef, the bay leaf, the wine—every bit had to be cooked to perfection. Keeping it waiting was unthinkable. And yet, naturally, tonight of all nights, out they went, and back they came late, and dishes had to be sent out again, dishes had to be kept warm; the Bœuf en Daube would be utterly ruined.
danish_before_fix: Og mens Jasper gik med beskeden, sagde hun til Rose, at hun, hvis hun havde lyst, kunne vælge de smykker, hendes mor skulle have på. Når der skulle sidde femten til bords, kan man ikke lade tingene vente i det uendelige. Nu begyndte hun at blive irriteret på dem, fordi de var så sent på den. Det var tankeløst af dem; og oven i hendes bekymring for dem irriterede det hende, at de skulle vælge netop denne aften til at blive væk så længe, når hun så inderligt ønskede, at middagen skulle lykkes, eftersom William Bankes endelig havde sagt ja til at spise med dem; og de skulle have Mildreds mesterværk—Bœuf en Daube, en fransk oksegryde, langsomt kogt i vin. Alt afhang af, at retterne kom på bordet i det øjeblik, de var færdige. Oksekødet, laurbærbladet, vinen—hver en detalje skulle være tilberedt til perfektion. Det var utænkeligt at lade den vente. Og alligevel, naturligvis, netop i aften af alle aftener var de gået ud og kom for sent hjem, og retterne måtte sendes ud igen, retterne måtte holdes varme; Bœuf en Daube ville blive fuldstændig ødelagt.

english: Jasper held out an opal necklace; Rose a gold one. Which looked better against her black dress? Yes, which? said Mrs. Ramsay vaguely, studying her neck and shoulders in the mirror (but keeping away from her face). Then, while the children rummaged through her things, she gazed out of the window at a sight that never failed to amuse her—the rooks trying to make up their minds which tree to settle in. Each time, they seemed to change their minds and rise into the air again, because, she thought, the old rook, the father rook—old Joseph, she called him—had a very trying and difficult temperament. He was a disreputable old bird, missing half his wing feathers. He reminded her of some shabby old gentleman in a top hat she had once seen playing the horn outside a pub.
danish_before_fix: Jasper rakte en opalhalskæde frem; Rose en af guld. Hvilken tog sig bedst ud mod hendes sorte kjole? Ja, hvilken? sagde fru Ramsay adspredt og betragtede sin hals og sine skuldre i spejlet (men holdt sig fra at se på sit ansigt). Så, mens børnene rodede i hendes ting, så hun ud af vinduet på et syn, der aldrig undlod at more hende—rågerne, som forsøgte at bestemme sig for, hvilket træ de skulle slå sig ned i. Hver gang så de ud til at skifte mening og løfte sig til vejrs igen, fordi, tænkte hun, den gamle råge, rågefaderen—gamle Joseph, kaldte hun ham—havde et meget besværligt og vanskeligt temperament. Han var en forkommen gammel fugl, der manglede halvdelen af sine vingefjer. Han mindede hende om en forhutlet gammel herre med høj hat, som hun engang havde set spille på horn uden for en pub.

english: “Look!” she said, laughing. They really were fighting. Joseph and Mary were fighting. In any case, up they all went again, and their black wings shoved the air aside and cut it into exquisite scimitar shapes. That movement of wings beating out, out, out—she never could describe it precisely enough to satisfy herself—was among the loveliest things of all to her. Look at that, she said to Rose, hoping Rose would see it more clearly than she could. Because so often your children gave your own perceptions a little push forward.
danish_before_fix: »Se!« sagde hun og lo. De sloges virkelig. Joseph og Mary sloges. Hvorom alting var, op fløj de alle sammen igen, og deres sorte vinger skubbede luften til side og skar den ud i udsøgte seglformer. Den bevægelse af vinger, der slog ud, ud, ud—hun kunne aldrig beskrive den præcist nok til at tilfredsstille sig selv—var for hende blandt det allerskønneste. Se der, sagde hun til Rose i håb om, at Rose ville se det klarere, end hun selv kunne. For så ofte gav ens børn ens egne iagttagelser et lille puf fremad.

english: “Choose, dearests, choose,” she said, hoping they would be quick.
danish_before_fix: »Vælg, mine skat, vælg,« sagde hun i håb om, at de ville skynde sig.
danish_after_fix: »Vælg, mine skatter, vælg,« sagde hun i håb om, at de ville skynde sig.

english: But she let them take their time over it. Rose especially she let pick up first this and then that, and hold the jewels against the black dress; for this little ceremony of choosing jewels, gone through every night, was what Rose loved best, she knew. Rose had some secret reason of her own for thinking it tremendously important to choose what her mother wore. What could the reason be? Mrs. Ramsay wondered, standing still while Rose did up the clasp of the necklace she had picked. Through her own past she could guess at some deep, buried, wholly wordless feeling that you had for your mother at Rose’s age. Like every feeling that someone has for you, Mrs. Ramsay thought, it made you sad. What you could give back was so inadequate; and what Rose felt was out of all proportion to anything she really was. And Rose would grow up; and Rose would suffer, she supposed, with such deep feelings. Now she said she was ready, and they would go down, and Jasper, being the gentleman, should give her his arm, and Rose, being the lady, should carry her handkerchief (she handed her the handkerchief), and what else? Oh yes, it might be cold: a shawl. Choose me a shawl, she said, because that would please Rose, who was bound to suffer so. “There,” she said, pausing at the window on the landing, “there they are again.” Joseph had landed on a different treetop. “Don’t you think they mind,” she asked Jasper, “having their wings broken?” Why did he want to shoot poor old Joseph and Mary? He shuffled a bit on the stairs and felt told off, though not seriously, for she didn’t understand the fun of shooting birds; that birds didn’t feel; and being his mother, she lived far away in another part of the world. Still, he rather liked her stories about Mary and Joseph. She made him laugh. But how did she know those were Mary and Joseph? Did she think the same birds came to the same trees every night? he asked. But at this point, all of a sudden, she stopped paying him the slightest attention, the way grown-ups always did. She was listening to a clatter in the hall.
danish_before_fix: Men hun lod dem tage sig god tid. Især lod hun Rose tage først det ene og så det andet og holde smykkerne op mod den sorte kjole; for denne lille ceremoni med at vælge smykker, som blev gennemført hver aften, var det, Rose holdt allermest af, vidste hun. Rose havde en hemmelig grund af sin egen til at synes, det var overordentlig vigtigt at vælge, hvad hendes mor skulle have på. Hvad kunne grunden være? undrede fru Ramsay sig, mens hun stod stille, medens Rose lukkede låsen på den halskæde, hun havde valgt. Gennem sin egen fortid kunne hun ane en dyb, begravet, helt ordløs følelse, som man nærede for sin mor i Roses alder. Som enhver følelse, nogen nærer for én, tænkte fru Ramsay, gjorde den én ked af det. Det, man kunne give igen, var så utilstrækkeligt; og det, Rose følte, stod ikke i nogen forhold til noget, hun virkelig var. Og Rose ville vokse op; og Rose ville lide, antog hun, med så dybe følelser. Nu sagde hun, at hun var klar, og de ville gå ned, og Jasper, som var herren, skulle række hende sin arm, og Rose, som var damen, skulle bære hendes lommetørklæde (hun rakte hende lommetørklædet), og hvad ellers? Å ja, det kunne blive koldt: et sjal. Vælg et sjal til mig, sagde hun, for det ville glæde Rose, som uundgåeligt kom til at lide så meget. »Der,« sagde hun og standsede ved vinduet på afsatsen, »nu er de der igen.« Joseph var landet i toppen af et andet træ. »Tror du ikke, de har det dårligt,« spurgte hun Jasper, »med at få deres vinger brækket?« Hvorfor ville han skyde stakkels gamle Joseph og Mary? Han flyttede sig lidt rundt på trappen og følte sig irettesat, om end ikke alvorligt, for hun forstod ikke det sjove ved at skyde fugle; at fugle ikke følte noget; og som hans mor levede hun langt borte i en anden del af verden. Alligevel kunne han ret godt lide hendes historier om Mary og Joseph. Hun fik ham til at le. Men hvordan vidste hun, at det var Mary og Joseph? Troede hun, at de samme fugle kom til de samme træer hver aften? spurgte han. Men på dette tidspunkt holdt hun pludselig op med at give ham den mindste opmærksomhed, sådan som voksne altid gjorde. Hun lyttede til en larm nede i hallen.

english: “They’re back!” she exclaimed, and immediately she felt far more annoyed with them than relieved. Then she wondered: had it happened? She would go down, and they would tell her—but no. With all these people around, they couldn’t tell her anything. So she had to go down, start dinner, and wait. And like some queen who finds her people gathered in the hall, gazes down at them, descends among them, silently acknowledges their tributes, and accepts their devotion and their bowing down before her (Paul kept perfectly still and looked straight ahead as she went by), she came downstairs and crossed the hall, bowing her head ever so slightly, as though accepting what they couldn’t say: their tribute to her beauty.
danish_before_fix: »De er kommet tilbage!« udbrød hun, og straks følte hun sig langt mere irriteret på dem end lettet. Så undrede hun sig: var det sket? Hun ville gå ned, og de ville fortælle hende det—men nej. Med alle de mennesker omkring kunne de ikke fortælle hende noget. Så hun måtte gå ned, sætte middagen i gang og vente. Og som en dronning, der finder sit folk samlet i salen, ser ned på dem, stiger ned iblandt dem, tavst anerkender deres hyldest og modtager deres hengivenhed og deres bukken for hende (Paul stod ganske stille og så lige frem, da hun gik forbi), kom hun ned ad trappen og gik gennem hallen og bøjede hovedet ganske let, som om hun tog imod det, de ikke kunne sige: deres hyldest til hendes skønhed.

english: But she stopped. Something was burning. Could they have let the Bœuf en Daube boil too long? she wondered. Please heaven, no! And then the great clanging of the gong announced, solemnly and with authority, that everyone scattered through the house—in attics, in bedrooms, on little perches of their own, reading, writing, giving their hair a final smoothing, or doing up their dresses—must leave all that, and the little odds and ends on their washstands and dressing tables, and the novels on their bedside tables, and the diaries that were so private, and gather in the dining room for dinner.
danish_before_fix: Men hun standsede. Der brændte noget på. Kunne de have ladet Bœuf en Daube koge for længe? undrede hun sig. Gud forbyde! Og så meddelte den store gongong højtideligt og med autoritet, at alle, der var spredt rundt i huset—på loftsrum, i soveværelser, på små siddepinde af deres egne, læsende, skrivende, i færd med at glatte håret en sidste gang eller knappe kjolen—måtte forlade alt det og de små ting på deres vaskeborde og toiletborde og romanerne på deres natborde og de dagbøger, der var så private, og samles i spisestuen til middag.

english: Lily Briscoe watched her drift off into that strange no-man’s-land where no one can follow. Yet when people go there, it chills those watching so much that they always try, at least, to keep them in sight—the way you watch a ship fading until its sails have dropped below the horizon.
danish_before_fix: Lily Briscoe så hende glide ind i det mærkelige ingenmandsland, hvor ingen kan følge med. Men når folk begiver sig derhen, kulder det de tilskuere så meget, at de altid forsøger, i det mindste, at holde dem i syne — som man følger et skib, der forsvinder, indtil dets sejl er sunket under horisonten.

english: What utter damned nonsense they talk, Charles Tansley thought, and set his spoon down exactly in the center of his plate, which he had scraped clean—as though, it struck Lily (he sat across from her, his back to the window, squarely in the middle of the view), he meant to make quite certain of his meals. Everything about him had that same thin rigidity, that same bare lack of grace. And yet the fact remained that it was nearly impossible to dislike anybody once you looked at them. She liked his eyes. They were blue, set deep, and frightening.
danish_before_fix: For noget vrøvl de snakker, tænkte Charles Tansley og lagde sin ske nøjagtigt midt på sin tallerken, som han havde skrabet ren — som om, det slog Lily (han sad overfor hende med ryggen til vinduet, lige midt i udsigten), han ville sikre sig sine måltider. Alt ved ham havde den samme tynde stivhed, den samme nøgne mangel på ynde. Og alligevel var det en kendsgerning, at det næsten var umuligt at mislike nogen, når man først så på dem. Hun kunne lide hans øjne. De var blå, dybtliggende og skræmmende.

english: He had no intention of talking the kind of nonsense these people wanted from him. He wasn’t going to let these silly women patronize him. He had been up in his room reading, and now that he had come down it all struck him as silly, shallow, flimsy. What did they dress up for? He had come down in his everyday clothes; he had no evening clothes to put on. “You never get anything worth having in the mail”—that was just the kind of thing they always said. They got men to say things like that. Well, yes, it was more or less true, he thought. From one year’s end to the next they never got anything worth having. All they did was talk, talk, talk, eat, eat, eat. The women were to blame. With all their “charm,” all their silliness, women made civilization impossible.
danish_before_fix: Han havde ingen intention om at sige den slags vrøvl, som disse mennesker ville have af ham. Han ville ikke lade disse tåbelige kvinder nedladende behandle ham. Han havde siddet oppe på sit værelse og læst, og nu da han var kommet ned, forekom det hele ham fjollet, overfladisk, spinkelt. Hvad pyntede de sig for? Han var kommet ned i sit hverdagstøj; han havde intet aftentøj at tage på. »Man får aldrig noget, der er værd at have, med posten« — det var netop den slags, de altid sagde. De fik mænd til at sige den slags. Nå, jo, det var mere eller mindre sandt, tænkte han. Fra det ene års ende til det næste fik de aldrig noget, der var værd at have. Alt, de gjorde, var at snakke, snakke, snakke, spise, spise, spise. Det var kvindernes skyld. Med al deres »charme«, al deres fjollethed gjorde kvinder civilisation umulig.

english: In spite of his eyes—but then, look at his nose, look at his hands—he really was, Lily Briscoe thought, the most charmless human being she had ever come across. So why did she care what he said? Women can’t write, women can’t paint—what did it matter, coming from him? Obviously he didn’t believe it; for some reason it was useful to him, and that was why he said it. Then why did her whole being bend down, like wheat in the wind, and only lift itself back up out of that humiliation by a huge and rather painful effort? She had to make that effort again. There’s the sprig on the tablecloth. There’s my painting. I have to move the tree to the middle. That’s what matters—nothing else. Couldn’t she just keep a firm grip on that, she asked herself, and not lose her temper, not argue—and if she wanted a bit of revenge, get it by laughing at him?
danish_before_fix: På trods af hans øjne — men så se på hans næse, se på hans hænder — var han virkelig, tænkte Lily Briscoe, det mest charmeløse menneske, hun nogensinde var stødt på. Så hvorfor brød hun sig om, hvad han sagde? Kvinder kan ikke skrive, kvinder kan ikke male — hvad betød det, når det kom fra ham? Han troede det åbenbart ikke selv; af en eller anden grund var det nyttigt for ham, og derfor sagde han det. Hvorfor så bøjede hele hendes væsen sig ned, som hvede i vinden, og rejste sig kun igen fra den ydmygelse ved en kæmpemæssig og ret smertefuld anstrengelse? Den anstrengelse måtte hun gøre igen. Der er kvisten på dugen. Der er mit maleri. Jeg må flytte træet ind til midten. Det er det, der betyder noget — ikke andet. Kunne hun ikke bare holde fast i det, spurgte hun sig selv, og ikke miste besindelsen, ikke diskutere — og hvis hun ville have en smule hævn, få den ved at le af ham?

english: He was annoyed that she had made him talk like that, and with Mrs. Ramsay listening. If only he could be up in his room, alone, working, he thought—among his books. That was where he was comfortable. And he had never owed anyone a penny; since the age of fifteen he had never cost his father a penny; he had helped out at home from his savings; he was paying for his sister’s schooling. All the same, he wished he had known how to give Miss Briscoe a proper answer, and that it hadn’t come out so abruptly. “You’d be sick.” If only he could think of something to say to Mrs. Ramsay, something to show her he wasn’t just a dry prig—which was what they all took him for. He turned toward her. But she was talking to William Bankes about people he had never heard of.
danish_before_fix: Han var irriteret over, at hun havde fået ham til at tale sådan, og med fru Ramsay som tilhører. Hvis han bare kunne sidde oppe på sit værelse, alene, og arbejde, tænkte han — blandt sine bøger. Det var dér, han følte sig tilpas. Og han havde aldrig skyldt nogen en øre; siden han var femten år, havde han aldrig kostet sin far en øre; han havde hjulpet hjemmet fra sine opsparede penge; han betalte for sin søsters skolegang. Alligevel ville han ønske, at han havde vidst, hvordan han skulle give frøken Briscoe et ordentligt svar, og at det ikke var kommet så bratt. »De ville blive søsyg.« Hvis han bare kunne finde på noget at sige til fru Ramsay, noget, der kunne vise hende, at han ikke bare var en tør pedant — hvad de alle tog ham for. Han vendte sig mod hende. Men hun talte med William Bankes om folk, han aldrig havde hørt om.

english: “Oh,” Mrs. Ramsay said, slightly startled. “No,” she added, thinking that she didn’t know this Carrie with her new billiard room. But how strange it was, she said again—which amused Mr. Bankes—that they should still be carrying on there. It was extraordinary to think that they had managed to keep on living all these years while she had thought of them barely once in all that time. And what a lot had happened in her own life over those same years. Then again, maybe Carrie Manning hadn’t thought about her either. It was a strange thought, and not a pleasant one.
danish_before_fix: »Åh,« sagde fru Ramsay, lidt forskrækket. »Nej,« tilføjede hun og tænkte, at hun ikke kendte denne Carrie med sit nye billardværelse. Men hvor mærkeligt det var, sagde hun igen — hvilket morede hr. Bankes — at de stadig skulle holde det gående dér. Det var ekstraordinært at tænke på, at de havde klaret at leve videre alle disse år, mens hun knap havde tænkt på dem en eneste gang i al den tid. Og hvor meget der var sket i hendes eget liv i de samme år. Men så, måske havde Carrie Manning heller ikke tænkt på hende. Det var en mærkelig tanke og ikke en behagelig en.

english: “I’m so sorry,” Mrs. Ramsay said, finally turning to him. He felt stiff and barren, like a pair of boots that has been drenched and then dried out, so you can hardly squeeze your feet into them. But squeeze his feet in he must. He must force himself to talk. If he wasn’t very careful, she would see through this betrayal of his—see that he didn’t care two straws about her—and that would be anything but pleasant, he thought. So he inclined his head politely toward her.
danish_before_fix: »Jeg er så ked af det,« sagde fru Ramsay og vendte sig endelig mod ham. Han følte sig stiv og gold, som et par støvler, der har været gennemblødt og så tørret ud, så man næsten ikke kan presse fødderne ned i dem. Men presse fødderne ned i dem måtte han. Han måtte tvinge sig selv til at tale. Hvis han ikke var meget forsigtig, ville hun gennemskue dette forræderi af hans — se, at han ikke brød sig to strå om hende — og det ville være alt andet end behageligt, tænkte han. Så han bøjede høfligt hovedet mod hende.

Så han bøjede høfligt hovedet mod hende.

english: Lily Briscoe knew all that. Sitting across from him, couldn’t she see it, as if in an X-ray, the ribs and thighbones of the young man’s craving to impress, lying dark inside the mist of his flesh—that thin mist convention had spread over his burning urge to break into the conversation? But why, she thought, narrowing her Chinese eyes and remembering how he sneered at women—“can’t paint, can’t write”—why should I help him find relief?
danish_before_fix: Lily Briscoe vidste alt dette. Da hun sad overfor ham, kunne hun ikke se det som i et røntgenbillede, ribbenene og lårbenene af den unge mands higen efter at imponere, liggende mørke inde i tågen af hans kød — den tynde tåge, konventionen havde bredt over hans brændende trang til at bryde ind i samtalen? Men hvorfor, tænkte hun, mens hun knebede sine kinesiske øjne sammen og huskede, hvordan han hånede kvinder — »kan ikke male, kan ikke skrive« — hvorfor skulle jeg hjælpe ham til lettelse?
danish_after_fix: Lily Briscoe vidste alt dette. Men hvorfor, tænkte hun, mens hun kneb sine kinesiske øjne sammen og huskede, hvordan han hånede kvinder — »kan ikke male, kan ikke skrive« — hvorfor skulle jeg hjælpe ham til at få lettelse?

english: “Tell me now …” he said. And so they argued about politics. Lily looked at the leaf on the tablecloth; Mrs. Ramsay left the argument wholly to the two men and wondered why the talk bored her so much, and she looked down the table at her husband and wished he would say something. Just one word, she told herself. If he said anything at all, it would change everything. He got to the heart of things. He cared about the fishermen and their pay. Thinking about them kept him awake at night. When he spoke, everything was different; you didn’t feel, then, please God don’t let them see how little I care—because you did care. Then she realized that she was waiting for him to speak because she admired him so much, and she felt as though someone had been praising her husband and their marriage to her face, and she glowed all over, never noticing that the praise had been her own. She looked at him, expecting to see all this in his face; surely he would be looking magnificent. … Not in the slightest! His face was screwed up; he was scowling and frowning and going red with rage. What on earth was the matter? she wondered. What could it possibly be? Only that poor old Augustus had asked for a second plate of soup—nothing more. It was unthinkable, it was loathsome (he signaled this to her across the table) that Augustus should be starting on his soup all over again. He hated people eating after he had finished. She watched his anger leap into his eyes, into his forehead, like a pack of hounds, and she knew that any moment something violent would burst out, and then—but thank goodness! she saw him take hold of himself and jam a brake on the wheel, and his whole body seemed to throw off sparks, but no words. He sat there scowling. He had said nothing, he wanted her to note. She should give him credit for that! But after all, why shouldn’t poor Augustus ask for more soup? All he had done was touch Ellen’s arm and say:
danish_before_fix: »Fortæl mig nu …« sagde han. Og så diskuterede de politik. Lily så på bladet på dugen; fru Ramsay overlod diskussionen helt til de to mænd og undrede sig over, hvorfor samtalen kedede hende så meget, og hun så ned ad bordet på sin mand og ønskede, at han ville sige noget. Bare ét ord, sagde hun til sig selv. Hvis han sagde noget som helst, ville det ændre alting. Han gik til sagens kerne. Han bekymrede sig om fiskerne og deres løn. At tænke på dem holdt ham vågen om natten. Når han talte, var alt anderledes; man følte ikke da, Gud give, de ikke ser, hvor lidt jeg bryder mig — for man bekymrede sig. Så indså hun, at hun ventede på, at han skulle tale, fordi hun beundrede ham så meget, og hun følte, som om nogen havde rost hendes mand og deres ægteskab lige op i ansigtet på hende, og hun glødede over hele kroppen uden at bemærke, at rosen havde været hendes egen. Hun så på ham og forventede at se alt dette i hans ansigt; han ville sikkert se storslået ud. … Ikke det mindste! Hans ansigt var fortrukket; han rynkede panden og skulede og var ved at blive rød af raseri. Hvad i alverden var der i vejen? undrede hun sig. Hvad kunne det dog være? Kun at stakkels gamle Augustus havde bedt om en tallerken suppe mere — ikke andet. Det var utænkeligt, det var afskyeligt (han signalerede det til hende henover bordet), at Augustus skulle begynde på sin suppe forfra. Han hadede, at folk spiste, efter at han selv var færdig. Hun så hans vrede springe op i hans øjne, op i hans pande, som en flok hunde, og hun vidste, at hvad øjeblik det skulle være, ville noget voldsomt bryde ud, og så — men Gud ske lov! hun så ham tage sig sammen og sætte en bremse på hjulet, og hele hans krop syntes at sprøjte gnister, men ingen ord. Han sad og skulede. Han havde ikke sagt noget, ville han have hende til at bemærke. Hun burde give ham kredit for det! Men hvorfor skulle stakkels Augustus egentlig ikke bede om mere suppe? Alt, han havde gjort, var at røre ved Ellens arm og sige:

english: “Ellen, please, another plate of soup”—and at that Mr. Ramsay had scowled like that.
danish_before_fix: »Ellen, vær så venlig, en tallerken suppe til« — og ved det havde hr. Ramsay skuet sådan.
danish_after_fix: »Ellen, vær så venlig, en tallerken suppe til« — og ved det havde hr. Ramsay skulet sådan.

english: Well, why not? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. Surely they could let Augustus have soup if he wanted soup. He couldn’t stand people wallowing in their food, Mr. Ramsay frowned back. He couldn’t stand everything dragging on for hours this way. But he had kept himself under control, Mr. Ramsay wanted her to note, revolting as it was to watch. But why make it so obvious? Mrs. Ramsay demanded. (They were looking at each other down the length of the table, sending these questions and answers back and forth, each knowing precisely what the other felt.) Everyone could see it, Mrs. Ramsay thought. There was Rose, staring at her father; there was Roger, staring at his father; another second and they would both be doubled up with laughter, she knew—and so she said quickly (and it was high time):
danish_before_fix: Nå, hvorfor ikke? forlangte fru Ramsay at vide. Man kunne da vel lade Augustus få suppe, hvis han ville have suppe. Han kunne ikke udstå, at folk svælgede i deres mad, rynkede hr. Ramsay brynene tilbage. Han kunne ikke udstå, at alting trak ud i timevis på den måde. Men han havde holdt sig under kontrol, ville hr. Ramsay have hende til at bemærke, så modbydeligt som det end var at se på. Men hvorfor gøre det så tydeligt? forlangte fru Ramsay at vide. (De så på hinanden ned langs bordets længde og sendte disse spørgsmål og svar frem og tilbage, begge vidende præcis, hvad den anden følte.) Alle kunne se det, tænkte fru Ramsay. Der sad Rose og stirrede på sin far; der sad Roger og stirrede på sin far; endnu et sekund, og de ville begge ligge dobbelt af grin, vidste hun — og så hun sagde hurtigt (og det var på høje tid):

(De så på hinanden ned langs bordets længde og sendte disse spørgsmål og svar frem og tilbage, begge vidende præcis, hvad den anden følte.) Alle kunne se det, tænkte fru Ramsay.
